blocks.content: Recognize GPS requirements and WAAS concept.

items.definition: A GPS receiver needs at least 4 satellites to compute 3D position (latitude, longitude, and altitude). WAAS augments this for precision approach accuracy — horizontal and vertical.
items.analogy: Three satellites give you a flat X/Y fix; the fourth satellite adds altitude — like a fourth wall that completes a box.

items.definition: An FAA ground-based correction system that broadcasts GPS correction data via geostationary satellites, improving GPS accuracy to approximately 1 meter horizontally and 1.5 meters vertically — sufficient for LPV precision approach guidance.
items.analogy: Like a spell-checker for GPS — it identifies and corrects signal errors in real time, making the answer more precise.

blocks.question: How many satellites must a GPS receiver track to compute 3D navigation with WAAS?
blocks.feedback: Four satellites are the minimum for 3D GPS: three to solve the 2D position and one additional to solve for altitude. WAAS provides ground-based differential correction to improve the accuracy of that 3D fix.

blocks.question: What is WAAS and what does it do for GPS navigation?
choices: An airborne sensor that detects satellite failures and alerts the crew
A military encryption system that restricts GPS accuracy for civilian use
A ground-based correction system that improves GPS accuracy for precision approach guidance
A backup navigation system that operates independently of GPS satellites
blocks.feedback: WAAS is an FAA ground network (not airborne) that corrects GPS signal errors. The corrections are uplinked to geostationary satellites and broadcast to suitably equipped aircraft, enabling sub-meter accuracy for LPV and other precision RNAV approaches.
